notes.meaning: God pronounces a sharp warning of judgment on the rulers of Judah, calling them bad shepherds. Leaders were supposed to feed, protect, and guide the people, but instead they harmed them and scattered them. God views His people as sheep belonging to His own pasture, so He will hold unfaithful leaders accountable.

The Lord confronts these rulers for completely failing in their sacred duty. He uses a play on words: because they did not attend to the flock with loving care, He will now attend to them with punishment. Leaders who abuse their power cannot escape God's justice.

God promises that He Himself will step in to do what the failed shepherds refused to do. He will gather the survivors of His flock from all the foreign countries where they were driven into exile, which means being forced away from their homeland. When brought back to their own home, they will feel safe, flourish, and grow in number.

God promises to appoint faithful leaders who will truly feed and protect His people. Under their care, the people will no longer live in constant dread of outside enemies or corrupt rulers. Not a single person in the flock will be lost or left behind.

God points to a coming King from King David's family line, calling Him a righteous Branch. Even though David's royal dynasty looked like a chopped-down tree stump, a fresh and holy shoot would rise from it. This promised King, the Messiah, will reign with true wisdom, administering justice and fairness across the land.

Under this King's reign, God's people will finally enjoy complete safety and peace. He will be known by the sacred name 'The LORD Our Righteousness,' meaning that God's people are made right and guilt-free before Him through this King. His perfect life and obedience become the basis of their peace with God.

differ.view: Some interpreters in this tradition read the title as God naming the King the giver of well-being, rather than a proof text for the doctrine of credited righteousness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue the name reflects the King's fair social policies that bring national stability, rather than personal spiritual justification.

notes.meaning: God declares that a coming rescue will be so wonderful that it will outshine the famous story of Israel leaving Egypt. In future days, people will no longer swear by the Lord who brought their ancestors out of Egyptian slavery. Instead, they will praise Him for gathering them out of Babylon and all other lands to live peacefully at home.

Jeremiah turns to confront the corrupt religious prophets and expresses deep personal grief. The prophet shakes all over and staggers like a drunken man because he is overwhelmed by God's holiness and the awful judgment ahead. It crushes his heart to see God's holy name abused by religious leaders while ruin draws near.

The land of Judah is filled with unfaithfulness to God, seen both in worshiping false gods and in broken marriage vows. Because of this widespread evil and false swearing, God placed a curse on the country that dried up the green pastures with severe drought. The people use their energy and strength to rush after wicked schemes instead of doing good.

The Lord declares that both prophets and priests have abandoned godliness. They even brought their corrupt practices and false worship directly inside the holy Temple in Jerusalem. When religious leaders dishonor the place where God is worshiped, the entire nation is led into sin.

God warns that the life path of these wicked leaders will become like a dark, slick walkway. As they try to press forward, they will slip, lose their balance, and plunge into disaster. God has set an appointed time of punishment when their proud actions will finally catch up with them.

God compares the false prophets of the northern kingdom of Samaria with those in Jerusalem. The prophets of Samaria were foolish for openly worshiping the idol Baal, but Jerusalem's prophets did something far more offensive. They claimed to speak for the true God while living sinful lives and telling evildoers they were doing just fine, making Jerusalem as wicked as ancient Sodom and Gomorrah.

The Lord of Hosts announces a bitter sentence against these false prophets. He will make them drink poisoned water and eat bitter weeds as a picture of severe divine judgment. Because these leaders spread moral corruption across the whole nation, they will receive the heaviest share of God's wrath.

God warns the people not to listen to the comforting messages of these deceptive prophets. Their cheerful visions came entirely out of their own human imaginations, not from God's mouth. They promised peace and safety to people who openly rebelled against God, soothing sinners into ruin rather than calling them to turn from their evil ways.

God asks whether any of these flattering prophets had ever actually stood in His heavenly council. A true prophet must stand in the Lord's presence, listen to His true voice, and pay attention to His commands. Since these pretenders never spent time listening to God, their messages were purely human inventions.

While the false prophets promised calm and sunny days, God warns that His judgment is bursting out like a violent whirlwind. This storm of divine anger will swirl down on the heads of the wicked until God's full purpose is carried out. When the disaster strikes, the people will finally understand that God's warnings were completely true.

God exposes these teachers as self-appointed messengers who ran to speak even though He never sent them. He gives a simple test to tell true messengers from false ones: a true word from God calls people to turn away from their evil deeds. Because these men encouraged sinners to stay comfortable in their rebellion, they proved they were not God's spokesmen.

God challenges the foolish idea that He is only a local god who can see nearby things but not what happens far away. He fills both heaven and earth, meaning He is present everywhere and sees everything. No one can sneak into a dark corner to plot lies without God watching every single move.

God hears the pretenders who claim they received divine revelations in their dreams. These claims were dishonest inventions designed to make people feel comfortable in their sins. By spreading their own ideas instead of God's truth, they caused the people to forget God's holy character, just as earlier generations forgot Him while worshiping idols.

God draws a clear line between human dreams and divine truth. If someone has an ordinary dream, let him tell it as a dream, but anyone who has God's word must speak it faithfully. God asks what worthless straw has to do with nutritious grain, showing that human opinions cannot nourish the soul the way God's truth does.

God describes the tremendous power of His genuine word. It acts like a fire that can melt stubborn hearts and consume impurities, and like a heavy hammer that can shatter hard rock. While false teaching lulls people into false comfort, God's true word breaks through human pride and transforms the conscience.

Three times the Lord declares that He stands directly against these dishonest prophets. They stole phrases from true prophets, used their own clever speech while claiming God said it, and misled the community with reckless lies. Because God never sent or authorized them, their teachings offered zero real help to anyone.

The Hebrew word for a divine message also meant a heavy load or burden, and the people used this double meaning to mock Jeremiah's serious sermons as tiresome burdens. When they sarcastically ask what 'burden' the Lord has for them today, Jeremiah must tell them that they themselves are the burden. God is tired of carrying their rebellious behavior and will cast them off.

God warns that anyone who flippantly uses the phrase 'the burden of the LORD' to make fun of His words will face punishment. It does not matter whether the mocker is a prophet, a priest, or an everyday citizen. Treating God's holy message as a joke brings judgment upon a person and their entire household.

God teaches the people how to talk about His word with proper honor and respect. Instead of sneering about a 'burden,' they should simply ask what the Lord has actually answered or spoken. Joking about sacred truth turns a person's own words into a crushing weight of guilt and insults the living God.

God warns that if the people stubbornly keep using this mocking phrase after being commanded to stop, severe judgment will fall. God will pick them up like an unwanted load and throw them far out of His presence, along with the city of Jerusalem. The people who took proud comfort in their holy city will instead face lasting shame and disgrace that will never be forgotten.
